utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, we again received a couple of documents, copies of documents, with a short summary. They have been provided to the parties again so that they can decide what to do with it, and, as usual, the summary will be translated with priority. We will see the appropriate action is taken in order to achieve that. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, before we will continue, I'd first like to deal with a few procedural matters, mainly about exhibits. First, I'd like to address the parties in relation to Exhibits P1091 and P1092. On the 10th of March of this year, two clips after film were played in court. The first clip, played at transcript page 21116, showed a ceremony honouring 18 new so-called Chetnik Vojvodas. This was admitted under exhibit number P1091. The second clip, which was part of the same exhibit, showed statements by Vojislav Seselj and Radovan Karadzic when Dr. Seselj took the new Chetnik Vojvodas to Pale. This was played at transcript page 21118 and inadvertently assigned a different exhibit number, namely P1092.A. The Chamber hereby instructs the registrar to correct the record by reassigning to the second clip the correct exhibit number, that is P1091. Then next issue is the numbering of P292 and P389. A binder of telephone intercepts was tendered by the Prosecution on the 27th of September, 2004, and admitted as Exhibit P292. A CD of telephone intercepts was tendered on the 8th of November, 2004, and admitted as Exhibit P389. In order to identify and cite these intercepts more easily, the Chamber hereby instruct the registrar to number each intercept as a separate tab under the corresponding exhibit number. This change is to be reflected in the Registry's exhibit list which is to also contain a reference to the KID identification number of each intercept, since the number has often been used in the courtroom to identify specific intercepts. Then the next issue is a reminder of the 6th of June order on exhibits. The Chamber would like to remind the parties that in accordance with the Chamber's order on exhibits rendered on the 6th of June, 2006, all missing items and translations must be provided to the registrar by tomorrow, that is the 20th of June. And finally, the Chamber wants to set a deadline for submission of Mr. Krajisnik's documents. During his testimony, Mr. Krajisnik has provided a large number of documents. These documents were distributed to Prosecution and Defence counsel in order to determine which documents they wished to have translated and offered into evidence. The Chamber is hereby setting a deadline on Friday, the 23rd of June for the parties to submit those documents which they wish to tender into evidence. Of course, if translations are not fully ready, an extension of time can always be applied for. These were some of the procedural issues the Chamber wanted to address. Mr. Stewart or Mr. Josse, are you ready to start the re-examination of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I begin by handing to Mr. Krajisnik a binder of documents? In part, the place I'm going to take him on occasions has been marked, as happened during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were asked a number of questions about Sarajevo. I'd like to first of all take you to a document that is labelled "B1," which formed part of the agreed principles at Dayton. This is an English-language document. You have provided this. Where did you get it from, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comes from the material that I brought from Dayton. I think every participant had the same package of background material and brought it with them from Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mediators, the people who worked there, including representatives of the European Community and representatives of the U.S.; one of them drafted and proposed this. A similar proposal to this was topical when Sarajevo was discussed as a district.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The handwriting at the very top of this page belongs to whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I: Proposal for Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a matter perhaps of form and curiosity, how was this document translated for you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was actually translated. We made do somehow. Somebody who knew English interpreted it. There was no time to translate it for those who didn't speak English at the conference, but we got a translation later and I have a Serbian version. I don't know how come that you didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why do you say this document is significant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in Dayton, during the discussions, between our delegation and Mr. Holbrooke, our delegation, the delegation of Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is Republika Srpska, accepted this proposal and we believed that Sarajevo should be a district because we did not see any other quality solution. We also thought that Sarajevo was at that moment an obstacle to achieving an all-round solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where do you say this document fits into the Prosecution's suggestion that you wanted to see the city of Sarajevo divided?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way up to Dayton, the proposal of the mediators was not to divide Sarajevo but to transform it, with one-third of the inner city belonging to Republika Srpska and two-thirds to the Federation. And we always kept saying that just as there was an umbrella organisation over all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there should be an umbrella linking Sarajevo because many things in the workings of a town inevitably have to be dealt with jointly. Perhaps that is what they saw as a basis for their claim that -- in fact, I did advocate that we, too, have a right to certain neighbourhoods, parts, of Sarajevo, without dividing Sarajevo as it is divided today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the document that we see, to what extent did the Serbian side accept what it proposed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even back with the Cutileiro Plan, the Serb side had accepted this solution as a provisional one, pending a quality solution, namely that Sarajevo should be a district, because Sarajevo was the most difficult problem to solve. And it was always the greatest stumbling block because the Muslim side wanted all of Sarajevo to belong to them, and that's where the problem lay. We, on the other hand, thought that we were entitled to a part of it, and there is still a debate today in Bosnia and Herzegovina published in Slobodna Bosna, namely transcripts of the deliberations are being published from 1993, when the leadership discussed this. It is being published now. I have that article and I can produce it, if necessary; it's a debate on several pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could this have a number, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D253, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you have also produced for the Chamber's consideration what amounts, in part, to an interview with General MacKenzie on video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the interview is -- forms part, itself, of an extract from some sort of television documentary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. It's a whole film of which the statement of General MacKenzie is only a part, and that DVD is available; however, I was unable to open it on my computer. I was able to open only certain parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we're proposing to play a section, five to ten minutes, which includes this interview with General MacKenzie. Before we do that, Mr. Krajisnik, are you able to assist with who produced the programme that we are about to play?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't possibly know that. It's spelled out there. It was a broadcast that was seen in Yugoslavia, on TV. Somebody in Europe made it. I don't even know who the participants in that programme are, but it was shown on -- in prime-time in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and elsewhere, and that's why we sent this DVD as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it had been obtained by investigators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Our investigators got hold of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the programme is in English. It is subtitled, fully, as far as we can make out in B/C/S. At this stage, there is no transcript whatsoever. Your Honour perhaps, with respect, might need to give some guidance to the interpreters as to what they should do. As I say, I repeat, it's subtitled in B/C/S; it's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Translations and subtitles are known not always to be very precise, also because there is limited space to write down something. I would like to invite the interpreters, to the extent possible, to translate the English as they hear it into B/C/S. They might, however, face such problems, which is entirely understandable. So therefore, we will consider whatever you translate, because we can't slow down those speaking on this television -- on this clip. We'll take that as a very provisional translation, and the Defence is invited to have the English transcribed and to submit it for translation to CLSS so that we get a final translation. So whatever is translated now is only a provisional translation. Is there any comment from the interpreters on what I suggested, whether that it's workable?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's give it a try.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We haven't heard it yet, so we have no idea what the sound track is like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We don't know about quality, we don't know about speed of speech. Let's just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's fast. Let me warn the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Then it is undoable, especially without a transcript of the English in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If -- Mr. Josse, at least those who understand English can at least try -- I hope I can follow it, and I hope that my colleagues can follow it as well, but we're not even sure about that. Let's see how things work out, and you are -- the interpreters are excused even before we have started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "The Muslims have been represented as the victims and the Serbs as the aggressors. It should be remembered, however, the first bloodshed in the struggle was Serb blood. Two Muslim gunmen and one Croat shot the Serb Orthodox wedding party in the heart of old Sarajevo; the father of the groom was killed, the Orthodox priest was wounded. "The killing of Nikola Gardovic on March 1st was a prelude to the war in Sarajevo. Despite promises from the government, the killers, who were well-known, were not arrested. The following day, roadblocks were set up by both Muslims and Serbs. Unable to protect their -- civilian population, Serbs began to insist that predominantly Serbian areas of the city be controlled by their own police or that Sarajevo become a UN protectorate. Muslims insisted on the Izetbegovic government's right to control not only Sarajevo but all of Bosnia. To get the West to intervene, they needed to persuade western public opinion that the Serbs were aggressors. "[Indiscernible] -- and you can very easily see them as the aggressors. "The American press corps, the diplomatic corps, and also the foreign correspondents themselves are heavily influenced by what is said and what is done in Washington DC. What the State Department says is the most important thing. "In his autobiography, U.S. Secretary of State James Baker says that he instructed the press secretary, Margaret Tutwiler, to help Bosnian foreign minister, Hari Silajdzic, utilise western mass media to build support in Europe and North America for the Bosnian parliament. "There have been times in the posts and at networks [indiscernible] networks, there was clearly a pro-Bosnian Muslim bias, and they were egging their reporters on because it made a better story. It's a simpler story, it's a -- just Serb holocaust against the Muslims, and it's a civil war with atrocities on both sides. Even if you find out when there is a real reckoning of what happened, a preponderance of -- or a higher proportion of the atrocities were committed by the Serbs, it doesn't mean it wasn't a civil war. It doesn't mean that there weren't two sides of the story. "This is part of our history, it's part of our culture, it's promoted by the entertainment industry, and then the -- so in the scene of Bosnia, we had to have a good guy and a bad guy. And we like to have a good guy, so it was very easy there because -- wait a minute, the Muslims are the victims; the Serbs are the bad guys; and the Croatian are kind of" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could the video stop for just a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There seems to be a lot of material contained on this. I'm not sure what specific point it goes to with respect -- in what sense it's re-direct. It certainly appears to me to be what I would have expected to arise, if it arose at all, during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony. So I mean, I'm seeing a lot of people talking about a number of topics. I don't know what it's directed to. It's certainly the kind of thing we should have had the opportunity to see and consider and address if it's relevant at all, and I'm just not sure in context of re-direct what it goes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we have not heard any questions yet, so therefore -- but Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two comments. First of all, as the Chamber is aware, Mr. Krajisnik produced this as at an early stage; it was made available to my learned friends. They could have considered it. They could have dealt with, as the Chamber repeatedly made clear to my learned friends. That's my first observation as far to what they say. Secondly, we are introducing this as Mr. Krajisnik's counsel in the context of Sarajevo and the questions, the robust questions, the suggestions that were put to him so far as Sarajevo was concerned. And, as will become clearer in a few moments' time, it leads up to an interview with General MacKenzie in relation to the suggestions the Prosecution made which were refuted by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we've been -- the Prosecution has attempted to be as fair-minded and even liberal as possible with respect to the [indiscernible] evidence I hope during the course of this case. However, I have to point out, it is unfair to suggest that because Mr. Krajisnik repeatedly produced materials for often unknown reasons, each morning during the course of his case that we were expected to address each and every one without knowing what it was going to. So I don't accept that -- the fact that it came up in that context as being a reason why we, the Prosecution, was in a position to deal with it during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's cross-examination. I don't want to make a bigger issue out of this than it is, however -- and I'll wait to see what it supposedly goes to, but it does strike me that we are seeing a good deal of information that might need attention. And we'll certainly be asking the Court for the opportunity to do so if that's the way the Defence intends to use it. As Mr. Josse just pointed out, all we knew about this thing at the beginning was something about General MacKenzie, and it wasn't entirely clear what that was going to be about, nor could -- was everyone able to access it at the time as I recall. Again, I'm not trying to interpose any unnecessary procedural obstacle; I just want to keep this as fair as possible. And seeing this video at length, which appears to me to be something that would have been expected during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's examination-in-chief, I raise the issue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Without expressing on the size of the issue at this moment, the Chamber also waits to see what it goes to. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "To a certain -- line which was anti-Serb, as opposed to actually trying to create balance of what the Bosnians were doing at the same time. "The press would have us believe that the Serbs had seized two-thirds of Bosnia. The fact is the Serbs had lived in that territory for 1500 years, and the fact is they are farmers and they are spread all over the landscape, so they have always been on two-thirds of the landscape. "The statement that has become an absolute [indiscernible] that the Serbs have taken over 70 per cent of Bosnia, again the underlying assumption is that there were no Serbs in Bosnia before the conflict started, when in reality much of the land of Bosnia was Serb land before the fighting ever began. But the implication is that the Serbs dropped in from some other planet and just took over nearly two-thirds of the country. "Based on what he now calls highly biased reporting, Penny [phoen] became a hard-line critic of the Bosnian Serbs, whom he considered aggressive. In an influential opinion column in the New York Times, Penny and U.S. Air Force General Michael Dugan argued that Bosnian Serbs should be bombed by NATO. "I personally was responsible for perhaps one of the most important things the State Department did is labelling what was going on "ethnic cleansing." I had tried to gain that public opinion, and part of my job was to draft material for the spokesman, Margaret Tutwiler. And she was always looking for inflammatory material, but in any case my colleague in Belgrade sent me a cable one day saying the Serbs were doing what they described as ethnic cleansing. I thought: Okay, great. I'll put this into Margaret Tutwiler's noon briefing. And to my surprise, no senior official took the words out. "The aggressors and extremists pursue a policy, a vial policy, of ethnic cleansing. "From that point on, the term 'ethnic cleansing' entered public discourse, but it was not in use before. And I think that that image somehow stuck, and then further down the road people tried to convert that into an image of genocide, and which doesn't really correspond to reality. "The reality was that all sides had been carrying out ethnic cleansing since the beginning of the war. "An example of it is that there's -- that's going on in all sides. It's going on in the United Nations Protected Areas, it's going on in the area of Bosnia. "Media perceptions influenced policies in western countries towards Bosnia in ways that widened and prolonged the conflict. The one force capable of keeping order in Bosnia might have been the Yugoslav army based in Sarajevo, which had the officers, men, and equipment to counter the many militias, Serb, Muslim, and Croat, that formed in the spring of 1992. General Kadijevic tried to do just that in meetings with leaders on all sides; however, under the threat of sanctions and pressed by the U.S. the JNA was forced to demobilise. In Sarajevo, most of the heavy weapons fell into the hands of Serbian forces, while in other areas Croats and Muslims inherited JNA weapons and armament factories. Instead of a standing army which could be held accountable for keeping order, a lightly armed force of UN peacekeepers was given the nearly impossible mandate of separating the warring sides. UN General Lewis MacKenzie criticised Serbian forces for their use of heavy artillery in the area of Sarajevo, but he also wrote later that most of the 19 cease-fires he had negotiated were broken by Muslim forces because their policy was, and is, to force the West to intervene. "There was an obvious short-term advantage in perpetuating the fighting in some areas in order to encourage the world to intervene. I don't think that's an illogical deduction at all, and I think most people would agree with that. "The fighting in Sarajevo was described by news organisations as a siege, but the reality was that of a divided city, its front line changed little in the course of the war. Serbs fired from areas they held into areas controlled by Muslims, and Muslim forces fired into areas controlled by Serbs. "And I think people don't really understand that in fact Serbian community in Bosnia suffered in exactly the same way that the other two communities suffered. "Veteran military correspondents such as Colonel David Hackworth at News Week observed that with 300 tanks at their disposal, 'taking out Sarajevo would be easier than sliding down a greased pole.' "General MacKenzie agreed that the Serbs could have captured the city in a matter of days early in the war, if that had been their intention. "Bearing in mind the extra JNA equipment that was there and the -- as admitted by the presidential side, the overwhelming superiority and gunnery and in tanks that was available in Lukavica then certainly a very -- a formidable assault could be made against the city with a fairly good chance of success. "Many observers wondered why a government under siege would shell its own airport. "On several occasions, the UN documented and reported and made clear publicly two or three days later that there were cases where the Bosnians had a mortar into areas where you wouldn't expect there to be military like the airport. "In his book, "Balkan Odyssey," Lord Owen wrote that Muslim forces would 'from time to time shell the airport to stop relief flights to focus world attention on Sarajevo.' "Sarajevo became after all a sort of icon of the problems of Bosnia because there was a satellite dish which was shipped in very early on in the crisis. It was easy, if you like, to have ready access to the war on a day-by-day, real-time, instant minute-by-minute basis, if possible. "And what was going on in Sarajevo was somewhat posturing from the international media. Whether we like it or not the presence of CNN, ICUTV [phoen], BBC, and the Sky News network and many others was an intimidating factor for any military operation going on in Sarajevo. That would be seen by the world, and the world would pass judgement based on what was going on in Sarajevo. As a soldier, it probably made a lot of sense to tie-up the media in Sarajevo, and then whatever your objectives were in the rest of Bosnia could be done without the presence of the media."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we heard various quotations there from General MacKenzie. First of all, an assertion that it was Muslims who broke Sarajevo's cease-fires. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said here by way of testimony was only what our soldiers had told us, when they were faced with the accusations leveled by the international community. They said that it was the Muslims who were breaking the cease-fire, that they were only responding. I really don't know what was correct, but I found this statement made by Mr. MacKenzie that is along similar lines, and that's why I presented it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we try to find out what period of time we are talking about? Is this 1992? 1992 only? Is it 1992 until 1995? I've got no idea. I think he was talking about 19 cease-fires. I don't know whether they can be located in 1992. If -- Mr. Krajisnik, if you do know, please tell us; if you don't know, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just know that Mr. MacKenzie was there in 1992, and that later there were other UNPROFOR commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it is your assumption that he only speaks about the time he experienced himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is my assumption, that he's talking about his own experience. But I don't know. I just know that he was there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was your understanding, Mr. Krajisnik, of what the general was saying that he had personally negotiated these 19 cease-fires, personally been involved in their negotiation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and that can be seen by what he says. Out of the 19 cease-fires, most were violated by the Muslims, not all of them. I know that he was there with our soldiers, and Mr. Koljevic had most contacts with him, as far as the civilian authorities are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He also stated that at the start of the war, had Serbian forces wanted to, they would have had no difficulty capturing Sarajevo. Are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a military strategist. It would be so hard for me to comment on that. I think that the intention really was not to take Sarajevo, and I think it is hard to take Sarajevo no matter how many tanks you have. Well, this is what I feel as a layman, but they are soldiers and they know better. However, the intention was not to take Sarajevo but to keep one's positions, as far as I know, that is. Now, whether the soldiers were planning something different, that I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about his assertion that it might have been to the advantage of the Muslims to keep fighting ongoing in Sarajevo in order to win western or further western support?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is with regret that I can say that that is certainly correct. Negotiations did not suit the Muslim side. They had a recognised, independent Bosnia-Herzegovina; their government was legitimate and legal, as far as the international community was concerned; and Bosnia was recognised as a unitary state rather than as a transformed state, which is what the other two sides had called for. Therefore, every conference was superfluous, as far as they were concerned. They wanted the situation to remain as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that CD have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just put one or two additional questions to this. Mr. Krajisnik, when we are talking about -- you said every conference was superfluous, as far as they were concerned. What was the percentage of the territory under Serb control by -- well, let's say, at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it must have been over 50 per cent. But, Mr. President, I'm going to tell you why I think that it was in the interest of the Muslim side not to have conferences held. They sought military intervention in order to deal with the rebel Serbs, or perhaps even the rebel Croats, to have someone handle them, to have NATO come in so that Bosnia would become peaceful in that way. That is why conferences did not suit them. That's why they thought that they should make a sacrifice and that they would show in that way that they were under threat, and that then NATO would move in; and that was the case several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there -- at that moment, were there municipalities where there was a Serb majority which were militarily controlled by the Muslim and Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say exactly. Even if that was the case, there were very few such cases; however, maybe I should add something, Mr. President. In the central part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the big cities, there was a large Serb population where Serbs were a minority. So there weren't municipalities, but there were a lot of Serbs who were there who remained in Muslim territory, that is, Zenica, Tuzla, Mostar, Travnik, and so on, in Sarajevo. So it wasn't municipalities, but there were a lot of them -- well Tuzla I know, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was the same on the other side, I take it that there were -- there was Muslim and Croat population in municipalities even forming a majority in those municipalities which were militarily under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, but in Serb territory, it was only Banja Luka, perhaps Prijedor, that were big towns; the rest were small towns. But you are certainly right. What was under Serb territory -- Serb control was, say, Vlasenica, with 8.000 to 10.000 inhabitants; and then perhaps Bratunac and so on. The only difference is in the size of the municipalities concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, the other difference is that -- isn't it true that, as you said at the beginning, that there were no municipalities with a Serb majority under Muslim and Croat militarily control? Isn't that one of the differences as well? Because that's how I started my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm saying that I don't know whether there were any municipalities that were majority Serb municipalities that belonged to them. If that was the case, there were perhaps only one or two such municipalities - I cannot recall now - because for the most part these were smaller municipalities. However, what is certain is that you're right, that there were some municipalities that were smaller indeed, but there were majority municipalities and they say -- came under the control of the Serb army. For example, in Tuzla, there were more Serbs than in three or four municipalities in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is where Serbs were a minority and also in Zenica. Big towns have a large population and you're in a minority. Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the issue of the Cutileiro Plan. You have produced, Mr. Krajisnik, at C2 a further map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we done with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be useful if I were to answer the first question. I submitted it to you today, and I see that you have made a proposal here to that effect, where I said that Sarajevo should be Serb. Is it necessary for me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Give me one moment. Yes, I was going to deal with that a little bit later, but I'm happy to deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right. We can do it later. Whatever you prefer. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to turn to a Cutileiro document that you have produced. It's in this particular bundle, C2, and it purports to come from an Institute for International Law and International Business Cooperation in Banja Luka in 1997 saying: "Dayton-Paris documents." Now, I have got a colour copy here, and perhaps that can be placed on the ELMO because that is really essential for an understanding of this particular map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst that is being done, Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps you could tell us about the institute and the obtaining of this particular document. If you could answer my question, then we'll look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a book, it was prepared by Dr. Vitomir Popovic and Dr. Vlado Lukic. Dr. Vlado Lukic was a participant in the Dayton Peace Conference. Within that book - and the name of the book is, "The Dayton-Paris Agreement," and it includes all the documents - there are certain maps that were - how should I put this? - made during the course of the negotiations and one of the maps is this map. I can bring the book here so that you can see that it's from this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, is the map in the book in colour?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is what it's like, just the way you see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why did you want to bring this map to the Trial Chamber's attention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was really surprised when I saw that this was turning into a problem here, namely what the Cutileiro map was; that is why I found yet another source so that you would see what was made public as the Cutileiro map. I remember this map. This is the only one I remember. I don't remember any other map. And we called this map the Cutileiro map. I really have to say that I never heard of any other map. Perhaps there were some working maps, but this was the map that we called the Cutileiro map, and on the basis of which we based our strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could we then have a bit more explanation on the map. What is green? What is red? What is white? What is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, there is an index. Perhaps the index could be brought into show, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps if we move it up a little bit. Yes. I now see that it seems the green is Muslim, red seems to be Croat, white seems to be Serb, where Sarajevo has its own --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Pink, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- pink colour. So let me just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the depiction of the corridor on the eastern side of Bosnia, according to this map? What do you say about that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you remember that map of mine, this is where the corridor should be, that would - how should I put this? - link Semberija up. I'm talking about the eastern part now. That's where the corridor would be, where in this narrow section it would link up Semberija. You didn't ask me about the corridor in Posavina, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't. But comment on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what I do not understand is who proposed this map? You say this is the Cutileiro map. Is this the map you agreed to? Because you always said: We agreed to the Cutileiro plan. Is this then the map you agreed to or how then should I understand this map? I have some difficulties in believing you would have done so, but -- so you say this is the Cutileiro map - it says it's from February 1992 - whereas I understand that if there was any agreement, that it was in March rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt, Your Honour? Do I understand Your Honour's question to be: Is the witness saying that this map that is on the ELMO was the actual map that was at the negotiations? Or is the question: Was it a map similar to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. My question is: What role did this map play? I can't imagine that during all of the negotiations there have been only one map on the table. I mean, we've seen many here already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if Mr. Krajisnik tells us this is the Cutileiro map, I'd like to know who presented this map. Was it Mr. Cutileiro, or the Serbs, or the Muslims, or the Croats? At what time? What role did it play in the negotiations? Just saying: Well, I had forgotten about it but this is the Cutileiro map is -- doesn't assist me in understanding what this map actually is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when Mr. Cutileiro decided -- or rather, when we reached that stage of establishing three constituent units, then the territories became bigger, so to speak. This was drawn by the late Mr. Darwin. I remember him. I remember his last name. He was an Englishman. And he said: Well, roughly these are the territories that we could have in larger terms. They are not 100 per cent Serb, 100 per cent Muslim, or 100 per cent Croat, but now you can have different exchanges, barters, and then you can turn them into compact units or other constituent units. You're right, no agreement was reached; this was a working map. And further work was supposed to be done on this and further agreements were supposed to be reached. Before that, all of us made our own proposals of maps and you saw those maps. That's why I don't know whether there were any other maps. Well, maybe there were. It's been a long time. But I know -- well, how should I put this? This is appropriate for the three constituent units. He identified territories that we could -- how shall we put this? - one constituent unit, the other constituent unit, and the third constituent unit. It is certain that this is the one and only and most important map. I don't remember any other map, and I attended all the talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I see when I'm trying to look at the map in more detail, is it -- do I see that Prijedor is here to become Croat? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prijedor -- well, the border is right next to Prijedor, and that's where Croat territory is. So you're right on that. This is the Croat part. And then there is this dot here, right on the edge of the yellow area or, rather, the red area that belongs to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any -- I still -- I do understand that someone presented this map as somewhere in the point of negotiating, the map which is, from what I see, quite different from many of the other maps that followed since then. Mr. Krajisnik, do you remember whether this was early February or late February or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that it was a basis for us on the 12th of May, when we were working on our strategic goals, and that's why I thought it was done -- or rather, that's why I said that was made before that -- well, it wasn't after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say this map was an inspiring moment for you to further think of your strategic goals to be achieved in these negotiations. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I said it very clearly. This map was before us when we formulated the strategic goals for the Assembly of the 12th of May. It was the Cutileiro map. And we said: Well, these are the goals with which we enter negotiations. Now, that is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you thought you had an agreement with the Muslims in relation to the negotiations that Mr. Cutileiro had chaired, how did that agreement relate to the map that is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of March, an agreement was reached on three constituent units; and the map was a working map that was supposed to be worked on, that is to say that it was a basis for us, namely that we were supposed to continue working on this map, that we should try to exchange territories, or perhaps make some improvements or prove that we have some rights somewhere, and so on and so forth. If you remember, we had one such round of talks with the Croats, and on the 12th of May we said that we would re-compose territories in Posavina so that we would get a corridor. I stated that, not Karadzic, and I provided copies to you here. So on the 18th of March an agreement was reached between the Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and the European Community, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could this map have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With the front page presumably as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the front page setting out in which book this map is found is part of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I next invite to you looks at C1, please, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that be distributed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is an extract from the Economist magazine of --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got C1; I just have C2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I nevertheless go back to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh I'm so sorry. Yes, it here it is. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you please be so kind to go back to the map, the coloured map, we had earlier? Because I had to find a few matters. You said this map, which you call the Cutileiro map - and let me just find your words literally -- referring to -- just trying to digest. When I tried to summarise your testimony, you said: "I said it very clearly. This map was before us when we formulated the strategic goals for the Assembly of the 12th of May. It was the Cutileiro map." And then you were asked by Mr. Josse: "When you thought you had agreement with the Muslims in relation to the negotiations that Mr. Cutileiro had chaired, how did that agreement relate to the map that is on the ELMO?" And I'm trying to understand. We have now a map in front of us, a map of February 1992, which is quite different from what I understand was the basic if not agreement, at least the starting point for further negotiations that was agreed upon on the 18th of March. And now you say on the 12th of May it was the February map rather than the 18th of March map which guided us in formulating our strategic goals. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- but we are of a view, Mr. Stewart and I, that perhaps Your Honour could point out to Mr. Krajisnik what the differences are between this new exhibit and what Your Honour had understood the position to be hitherto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have to look at the other maps. Perhaps I will do that during the next break to see where the differences are, but if you say it's the same, then I have perhaps -- better to compare them better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we are not saying they are the same; we are saying they are similar. We have not done a very detailed cross-referencing, so to speak, but clearly that needs to be the starting point bearing in mind the question Your Honour was formulating for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll compare them what D7 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: B, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll try to do that, and perhaps meanwhile you'll continue, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is another Cutileiro document, as I already said, that we would like you to look at, Mr. Krajisnik. And this comes from the Economist magazine of the 15th of December of 1995. It doesn't say that on the article, but we have checked it. And this is a letter to the editor of that publication from Mr. Cutileiro. It's not presently translated, so I'm going to read it out. Headed "Prewar Bosnia." It says, "Sir, in your article on Bosnia, November 25th, you say that in February 1992, before the war had started, Lord Carrington and I 'drafted a constitution that would have turned the country into a confederation of Swiss-style cantons. The Muslims refused to accept what they considered to be disintegration of Bosnia.' Not quite. After several rounds of talks, our 'principles for future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina' were agreed by the three parties, Muslim, Serb, and Croat, in Sarajevo on March 18th, as the basis for future negotiations. These continued, maps and all, until the summer when the Muslims reneged on the agreement. Had they not done so, the Bosnian question might have been settled earlier with less loss of mainly Muslim life and land. To be fair, President Izetbegovic and his aides were encouraged to scupper that deal and to fight for a unitary Bosnian state by well-meaning outsiders who thought they knew better." First question, Mr. Krajisnik: Does that support your view of what happened in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that all that Mr. Cutileiro stated here is absolutely correct, and that furthermore Mr. Izetbegovic, if he had been deciding alone, would have stuck to his promise. However, he was under pressure by some agencies to renege on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was my next question. Are you able to say who you think Mr. Cutileiro means when he talks of "well-meaning outsiders"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot call them outsiders, but I know that Ambassador Zimmerman certainly suggested to Mr. Izetbegovic that he should reject the agreement. However, Mr. Izetbegovic also had in his own circle people who were not accountable for anything, but they did advocate the rejection of any transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These people wielded certain power in relation to Mr. Izetbegovic. They had the possibility to influence him, and he was in a vice between his own desires and the wishes of outside policies, foreign policies. I know Mr. Izetbegovic -- I knew him, rather, and I spent quite a lot of time with him. And I know that if he had been alone to decide, he would have stuck to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D256, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to stick with the subject of Mr. Izetbegovic and look, please, at an interview that he gave in October of the year 2000, which is document F1 in your bundle, Mr. Krajisnik. This is a quite a long interview. There is only a short bit that I wish to ask you about. What publication is this from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a Sarajevo publication, a Muslim newspaper called Dani.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can -- would you read out what the title of the interview is, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The only kind of people I hate are traitors."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see somewhere in the introduction, about five lines down, a word that begins, n-a-j-e-k, and a sentence that ends in your name. Could you read that part out, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He confirms, in the most explicit way ever, that he found Krajisnik the easiest to agree with, and finally - and seemingly unconvincingly - response to all the critics who did not have any sympathy for him over the morning and afternoon opinions. And finally, after all these years, claims that he would rather form a coalition with the SDP than with the SDS or HDZ, on certain conditions that are such that they mean that he would actually never form such a coalition."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 19, which is the last page of this interview, in the far right-hand corner - it's been marked for your benefit, Mr. Krajisnik - we have a question that begins, "Jednom." Could you read the question and then the answer, but slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "You stated on one occasion - and correct me if I'm wrong - that of all the representatives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you found Krajisnik the easiest to agree with, to talk to. Why? Are Radisic and Jelavic nationalists?" This was the question. Izetbegovic answers: "Yes. I did say something like that. I have spent dozens of hours in difficult negotiations with Krajisnik. I shall never forget our lengthy tug of war over the Bosnian currency. That was real torture, but I had no feeling of hatred towards Krajisnik. The only kind of people I hate are traitors. That is due, probably, to my experience of prison. Krajisnik, however, was not a traitor. He fought for the Serbian people to the best of his understanding of that people and their interests. I will leave Jelavic and Radisic for some other time."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, may I seek clarification of one of the previous answers? You were asked by Mr. Josse whether the letter sent by Mr. Cutileiro to the Economist, whether that supports your view of what happened in the spring and the summer of 1992. Now, there is a lot said in this letter. It's clear that Mr. Cutileiro takes the position that if the Muslims would have stuck to an agreement, a three partite agreement, that it would have saved, as he says: "... so, the Bosnian question might have been settled earlier, with less loss of mainly Muslim life and land." . Where you said that this letter does support your view on what happened, would that include, I'm just asking, not to be confused about it, that it was mainly Muslim life and land that was lost by not settling earlier the Bosnian question? Would that be included or would that not be included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslim life also, there would be less loss of life, Muslim, Croat and Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm asking, Mr. Cutileiro writes, "mainly Muslim." I'm just asking you whether you agree with that or you disagree with that, that it was mainly Muslim life and land that was lost due to the late settlement of the Bosnian question. Nobody says, neither does Mr. Cutileiro say that there was no Serb life lost and no Serb land was lost, or Croat life was lost, but he says that it was mainly Muslim life and land that was lost. Do you agree with that or do you not agree with that? I'm just trying to find out to what extent you agree with what Mr. Cutileiro wrote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Cutileiro is right. The greatest loss of life and loss in general was on the Muslim side. I have to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And land as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as land is concerned, I have my reservations at that point, because Muslims lived in towns. As for life, Mr. Cutileiro is right, and I have to be honest and say that it's true. Although there was loss on other sides as well, but mostly on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse -- oh, I'm looking at the clock and see that it's -- we had a late start, so if you had -- I don't know. We started, due to technical problems, 15 minutes late, so if you would have for the next ten minutes, then you can continue and then we'll adjourn close to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask Mr. Krajisnik, he doesn't need to see the document, but it's for the Chamber's reference, P1213.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, you faced a number of questions, primarily from the learned Presiding Judge, about an issue to do with Russian-made automatic rifles. And if you look at your binder, could you turn to document I1, please? It should be in the binder in front of you, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, this is a document that appears to have an ERN number upon it. Notwithstanding that, how did you obtain this document, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document is filed as an OTP document. I found it in my documentation. It has a number, too. I don't know if somebody sent it. It has a number in the upper corner but, it also has an ERN number 005973. It's part of a report from the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you read out the title slowly, please? In other words, the words above the table.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Overview of weapons and equipment issued to staffs and units of the TO by the 5th Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind we don't have a translation, which line do you say is relevant to this issue of Russian-made automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Line 6 in the table. I can read what is written: "Automatic 7.62 millimetres, M49/57." It's a model, 49/57.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how -- what light does this show -- let me start that again. And what light does this shed on the issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we get all kind of confusion, could we -- and could you assist us, Mr. Josse, in identifying the issue? The issue was the interpretation, I think, of a report on weapons found in a motor vehicle; and the issue was, I think, that - but please correct me when I'm wrong - that this was understood, I think even by Mr. Krajisnik, as weapons that were old-fashioned. And that was the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The age of the weapons was the issue, as I recall it, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I remember with old automatic rifles. Yes. Then, that being the issue, Mr. Krajisnik, could you please respond to the question what the sixth line -- what light it sheds on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, those are automatic rifles with a drum, models from 49 to 57, and they originated in the Second World War. The ammunition is 7.62, and as we can see two blocks up, rifle 7.62 millimetres, automatic rifle. That is a new product and that one is an old product from 49 to 57, and it originated in World War II. Those are the rifles with a drum barrel that the TO had. They emerged at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how do you know that this refers to the weapons that are mentioned in P1213, the report to the minister of the interior in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only automatic weapons of Russian -- Russian-made were those with a drum barrel. And since what was written there was "Russian automatics," then I understood that to mean those with the drum barrel. In fact, my answer was that I didn't know anything about it. I just attempted to interpret what that was all about. These, too, are Russian automatics. That's what they were called, the drum-barrel ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could this have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you tell us what the other automatic weapons, rifles, what origin they have on this list? I don't know. It's difficult for me to read it, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to explain, Your Honour. The first one is a pistol, 7 - I think it says - 52. It was produced by the Crvena Zastava factory in Kragujevac. Then comes the pistol 7.65, automatic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The first, it say "pistol," and then could you read it? I have some difficulties in reading it. The first line is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With great difficulty, but I can see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does it say? The first word, what does that say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Pistol, 7.62 millimetres."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say this is a certain make. What makes you believe that this is a certain make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I had that kind of pistol before the war myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand you. What makes you believe that the pistol described in the first box is of - what did you say? Let me just have a look - is of a certain make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm telling you as a man who is not a military man, but I know that all these pistols indicated here, except the first, second, and third one, were produced by the military branch of the Crvena Zastava factory in Kragujevac and they were available on the market to people who wanted to buy weapons to have in personal possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say you can't learn this from the document, but it's general knowledge that leads to you conclude that this must be CZ-produced pistols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because Crvena Zastava had a very modern factory that produced weapons. For instance, the 7.62 rifle, it's in the fourth box, that's the Kalashnikov, the automatic. Crvena Zastava used to produce a modern automatic rifle using a Kalashnikov licence. That's a modern rifle, that one. Number 5 is PAP, 7.62; it's a semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm very much a layman in this respect. You say "Kalashnikov licence." May I then take it that it was -- Kalashnikov is a Russian firm but has given licences to other companies to produce -- I'm unfamiliar with the matter, so please tell me what it is. You say it's under Kalashnikov licence. What -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kalashnikov was a scientist, it's the name of a scientist, so that rifle was named after him. He came recently. He is 85 years old, and he gave Zastava licence to manufacture that. I know that as a citizen. And that was a lethal weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody had these Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you're telling me that in the fourth box the 7.62 millimetre automatic rifle was produced under Kalashnikov licence. Then if I understood you well, by CZ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there other licences given by Kalashnikov to produce Kalashnikov weapons, of Kalashnikov-type weapons I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know. You know, in the former Yugoslavia there was this distribution of military production. So something would be manufactured in one particular city, and in Zastava and Kragujevac it was that kind of small weapons, and then in Vitez, in Slovenia, everybody made whatever they were supposed to make. Somebody made tanks, and so on and so forth. Some made guns, cannons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was all Yugoslav-produced, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we now go to the sixth -- I'm not very familiar with these kind of matters, so I'm just trying to understand. Now you say the sixth box, that is Russian, 7.6. Could you first of all read what it exactly says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Automat 7.62 mm," that means millimetres. Then there is a capital "M49/57."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was produced in Russia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. They were just called Russian automatic weapons. These Automat Dobosar type, the ones with the drum barrel. Now, where was this produced, in Zastava? In Russia? Well, that's what they were all called, because they were old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Kalashnikov were never referred to as Russian rifles. What was the nationality of Mr. Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, automatic rifles, automatic rifles. What was said was automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's what box six says as well, "Automat, 7.62."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the ammunition is different, Mr. President, and they call them obtuse bullets. The model is different. Up here there is a rifle and down here there is an automatic weapon, "Automat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the fifth box, "PAP, 7.62." What does that stand for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a semi-automatic rifle. Semi-automatic rifle, 7.62. I think -- I think there was also manufactured by Zastava, Crvena Zastava Kragujevac, that is, as far as I know. And they were there only in the beginning of the war and later on there were only automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least it has become a bit clearer to me. Mr. Josse -- oh, looking at the clock, it's -- yes, I'm just trying to understand what conclusions I draw from this table in relation to the issue we discussed before. Then we'll adjourn until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Prosecution has provided the Chamber with the information that the document I1 was already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They helpfully informed us as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think it was attached to P741.1. And from the original, we see that the word "Automat" is used. That was the whole starting point on how to interpret what kind of weapon it would have been. The interpreters, when the issue -- when the issue was raised told us how to understand "Automat," it means even a translation in the sixth box where it reads, "Machine-gun," might not be because it's unclear whether it was a machine-gun or an automatic rifle so let's take that for granted. At the same time, the issue also might have been whether this relatively old weapon was still of any use during the conflict. At least I can imagine that that -- I mean, but perhaps we ask Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, you said this was weaponry from the Second World War, I think you said. What would be the relevance of weapons being that old, apart from that it's not state of the art?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, no. I was just talking about this type of weapon, that it went back to the days of the Second World War and we can see that it was manufactured after the Second World War, too. I had an uncle who was in the Second World War and he was in the army, and he had this kind of weapon, with a drum barrel. That's how I knew it was from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a lethal weapon but obsolete. You can actually kill a person with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but would it still be used? Would it still be used for military purposes? In 1992, would you still use that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at first, this did exist, but as soon as more modern things came in, these other ones disappeared. Everybody wanted to have a more modern weapon. I don't know what happened to the rest, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the old-fashioned weapons, would they still be distributed for use in the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I guess so, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because that's what is even P741 tells us, because that is a letter sent by Major General Talic to the 1st Krajina Corps command in which he explains that this is the weaponry that is -- that's weapons issued to units and TO staffs; in other words, to structures outside of the armed forces, since the beginning of the activities aimed at protecting Serbs from genocide in Croatia and the Serbian Republic. So I do understand from this letter, to which this list was attached, that it still could play an active role in hostilities. Or do I -- is this a wrong understanding of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Mr. President, the Territorial Defence was under the Yugoslav People's Army, but it was separate. I mean, it was a separate entity. When weapons are distributed, they are being distributed for the purpose of waging war, you're quite right, not for people to keep them at home. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I make an observation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst I appreciate that we have chosen to re-examine on this topic, bearing in mind the exchange between Mr. Krajisnik and indeed yourself in relation to these Russian automatic rifles, many of the questions, with respect, that Your Honour is now asking would surely be better asked of some of the many witnesses who appeared before there Chamber who are far more qualified to deal with what actually happened in the field than Mr. Krajisnik. The Chamber has heard from many people who were involved in the conflict on a daily basis, and the Chamber has heard from military experts who also, I suspect, could deal with this issue. Just an observation which might assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik has made it clear he's not a military expert. It's not in dispute that he physically wasn't involved in the fighting; that's one area that the parties are agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was, however, a possible suggestion of obsolete weaponry, which of course would tend to diminish the importance of the event that happened at that time. And Mr. Krajisnik was quite explicit on that, and very quickly -- and we now see that it's in evidence already and that the -- although perhaps being obsolete, that it was still at least in a document presented as a weapon which was actively distributed at the time. I think that's -- but if there is any further dispute of that, we'll further hear. Please proceed, Mr. Josse. One of the consequences is since P741 is already in evidence, number D258 would be vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that could be given instead to the next document which is H1 in your binder, Mr. Krajisnik. H1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is an interview with Mr. Krajisnik from Srpski of the 21st of December of 1992. And, Your Honour, what we have done is in fact the penultimate question and answer is the question and answer we are interested in. And if one turns to second page of this extract, that has been blown up to make it easier for all concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you've got it highlighted in yellow, Mr. Krajisnik. You've also got the blown-up portion. Could you read, please, that question and answer, slowly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "You know that the commission for human rights, the UN commission on human rights, even adopted a resolution blaming only the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina for genocide." That was the question. Answer: "The term 'ethnic cleansing' does not correspond, at least not entirely, to what is going on in the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we do not think that the Serbs - I'm taking them by way of an example - were expelled from Vitez or from Zenica, if they were enabled to move out peacefully or, rather, to go where they would be safer, the territory of Republika Srpska. I personally am against any form of coercion. I energetically condemn any attempt of forcible removal of people from their homes, centuries old. That is why this term, 'ethnic cleansing,' has to be taken with a certain reservation. It was used only in the report of Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the former Polish Prime Minister, who extremely one-sidedly, hypocritically, as if he were making this report through a commission, blamed only the Serbs in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you want me to read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember giving this interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember from this distance when I gave this interview, but I know that this was my position with regard to ethnic cleansing and the report of Mr. Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And does that differ from your position today?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as far as the Mazowiecki report is concerned, there is no difference. As for ethnic cleansing, I know what it means to leave your home. To this day, I am deeply opposed to any kind of forcible expulsions of populations because I believe that this is the gravest emotional upheaval that can befall a person. To this day, I sometimes have dreams of my village, although I was not ethnically cleansed; I just left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour now want this to bear the number D258?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it's a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honour. We are checking on the number right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution exhibit. Then we'll wait and see whether -- have you done with these documents or are you putting questions to Mr. Krajisnik about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not putting any further questions about this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, I'm trying to closely read what you said. You said: The term 'ethnic cleansing' does not correspond, at least not entirely, to what is going on in the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then you give the reasons. You say: "We do not think that the Serbs were expelled from Vitez or from Zenica," just giving an example, "if they were enabled to move out peacefully." This answer suggests that they did not take that opportunity to move out peacefully, or is this a wrong understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I said that people were happy when they left imperiled areas, when Serbs came to our territory. Perhaps that's even more important, a lot more important, than the reason why they had left because they managed to stay alive so people were happy. So, by way of reciprocity, I was thinking about this, and I was receiving information about it too, that that is the same way the Muslims in our territory felt, that they wanted to go to safer areas. I would be opposed to expelling anyone. That is the gist of what I said. I had the opportunity to observe Serbs and to draw certain conclusions on the basis of that. A lot of them had left Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that you say that if you finally decided to go to a safer place, then that is not ethnic cleansing. My next question would be: If you make life so miserable or if you make life so dangerous that--

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I -- may I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They are quite different in many ways, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll split it up. If you make life so dangerous, to start with that, that people have to -- that people are choosing to go to a place which is safer, would that -- and I'm trying to formulate my question as carefully as I can - would that exclude for the possibility that this could be ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a sensitive question, Mr. President. I am against any kind of coercion. It is hard to prove coercion, though, because it is mixed with objective and subjective reasons; and if you want to highlight something, you highlight subjective reasons. If you want to proceed in an objective fashion, you say: I am afraid because I am a minority. So it only depends on how many elements there are involved. I cannot be an arbiter to that, as to what prevailed in the minds of Muslims who left. If somebody made their life difficult on purpose, not due to the war -- the war brings about many difficult situations, but if somebody did that intentionally -- maybe this also happened to the Serbs in Zenica, I don't know -- well, thank God these people left and they stayed alive. It was different when people were being expelled by force, then you have a clear-cut situation. That is why I said that I was opposed to ethnic cleansing, and I compare that to the Serb side, not the Muslim side because I don't know what prevailed in their heart of hearts. They all signed that they wanted to leave and so on and so forth, and they were glad to leave and later they said they were ethnically cleansed. So it is very hard to deal with this. It is easy to create a difficult situation in a war. It is sufficient that there is a war going on, that is quite sufficient. There is no food, many things are lacking, that's sufficient for a person to want to leave. It doesn't have to be intentional; it can be unintentional, too. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The line you just spoke: "They all signed that they wanted to leave and so on and so forth, and they were glad to leave. And later they said they were ethnically cleansed. So it's very hard to deal with this," would that mean that it's, in your view, that it could not have been ethnic cleansing or that it's difficult to decide whether it was ethnic cleansing or whether it depended on the circumstances on whether it was ethnic cleansing? Could you give us your views on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be as objective as I can. At least it is not pure ethnic cleansing. I gave you the example of Pale. I talked to everybody about this, I asked everybody about this. There was no coercion, but later on some people came out and said that they were ethnically cleansed. So now you have to collect some kind of evidence to prove that that was not the case because everybody was fleeing from areas where they were minority. Now, perhaps somebody was forcing them, too, as you had put it, but it is sufficient for people to be in a minority and want to leave most towns. I cannot be the judge of that, what happened in a particular municipality, because I was not there, but I am trying to be as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, please proceed. And for your information, the interview is in P583, tab 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
