utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you referred earlier to the interview at the front of your bundle which is labeled A6, and you told the Chamber that you wish to refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is P1241. We do have further copies, although of course it was exhibited recently in the course of the cross-examination of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, page 5, the far right-hand corner, which is as much as anything is for the benefit of the interpreters, about halfway down that final column you have a passage, Mr. Krajisnik, that is highlighted. That passage was not translated by the Prosecution. It's not a criticism, it's just a fact. Could you read that passage out slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Thus, whose fault is it? Maybe it's rather the fault of their mentor than the fault of the Muslim side, although they too should have taken the war into account. But they are to blame when we are talking; when they are talking, we are to blame. And I'm not to go any further into that problem. The basic thing is, since the war was imposed, that the war has brought new realities. Unfortunately, the product of this new reality are many victims. Now, there are no Serbs in Central Bosnia, or at least there are a lot fewer of them. Maybe there are 100.000 of them in Eastern Bosnia, where there used to be Muslims, but nowadays, there are no Muslims there. Instead, they have fled to the central part of Bosnia. Now, simply, Serbs, Muslims and Croats have separated or, more precisely, Serbs separated from the others, because in the Federation there are still mixed enclaves. They have separated like oil and water, whether we like it or not. In every aspect of life, when you put -- when you fill a bottle half with oil, half with water, and you shake it, then it turns into one liquid; when you set the bottle down, then the layers separate. The former system used to hold it all together through different keys and a little bit of force, and thus we were 'mixed' as one whole."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So these were remarks that you made in 1995. How do they fit in, if at all, with the questions that you've been asked, both by the learned Prosecutors and by the learned Presiding Judge, about your view of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was trying to say here was that the war had created new realities. I didn't want to go into whether people were forced out of their homes, whether they were expelled or whether they left of their own will. But the fact is that there were no Serbs in Mostar, there were no more Muslims in Zvornik, and so on and so forth; and when I was saying that, I really meant that all three ethnic groups were in the same position. It would be very harsh to say that all the Serbs left Central Bosnia of their own accord, whereas all the Muslims had been expelled. I continue to believe that during the war all three ethnic groups suffered equally and the conditions that led them to leave their homes were much the same for all the three groups. Under the socialist system, there was a false appearance of brotherhood and unity where we were all as one. However, as soon as the war began, the underlying animosities came to the surface, leading to an all-out war among the three ethnic communities. Under the socialist system, in that era, there was great 'love' among the three groups; however, when the war began, it turned out to be completely untrue. They became enemies. I say that with regret but I have to say it because that's the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau was a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, you said: [In English] "Under the socialist system, there was a false appearance of brotherhood and unity where we were all as one." [Interpretation]: And a little further down you say: [In English] "Under the socialist system, in that era, there was great 'love' among the three groups." [Interpretation] Isn't this an oxymoron? You seem -- sorry, Mr. Krajisnik, I didn't let you finish, but you seem to be saying that there is a brotherhood which is imposed in a certain way by the socialist regime; and on the other hand, you were telling us that there was love in that society. Thank you. Please tell us if, yes or no, this is a contradiction in terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said love under quotation marks which maybe led you to misunderstand me. I believed all that. I believed that there could never be war between us, among us. I never believed that there was any hatred. I had friends among Croats, among Muslims. We were in a relationship of mutual respect, but it's simply hard to believe that hatred came to the surface out of nowhere when the war began. And it can't only be the fault of the leaders. As soon as the war began, people started remembering events and drawing on examples from a hundred years ago, and I realised that what I believed in, the love, the brotherhood, the unity, that all that was false. I realised that the so-called principle of the key, the proportional representation system, under which, if you had a Muslim director, the deputy had to be a Serb and so on, that principle ruled everything. There is no greater love than the love that links brothers; however, when they quarrel, their hatred can be as strong as their love used to be. And what we witnessed was enormous bloodshed. It's been 12 years since Dayton now, and still, today in those territories, the hatred lives on, the animosity lives on. In Mostar, in all the other places, there are no more any -- no longer any war criminals among them, but the animosity still exists. The people who say that everything is all right there are lying. There is a rift among the people. People are isolating themselves within their communities, even now, 12 years later. I cannot explain it. Maybe psychologists could have a go at finding an explanation for that. The easiest thing to say is that somebody else is to blame for all of that, that the war was not their fault; however, the seed itself had to be there, since it spread so fast. I don't know if I managed to explain. I have said here, in this interview, when we are discussing, it's their fault. When they are discussing, it's our fault. Everybody blames somebody else. If you listen to a Serb, the Muslims are to blame. If you listen to a Muslim, then the Serbs are to blame. It's always somebody else's fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no English translation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the microphone wasn't on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would you please re-ask your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say the following, Mr. Krajisnik. I wanted to ask you the following question, Mr. Krajisnik. I heard what you just told us and have listened with great attention, but I would like to know today, after all these years, in hindsight, were you able to find an explanation for this reoccurrence of hatred which caused so much suffering? We understood that everybody suffered. This is what we heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Muslim issue, the Croat issue, the Serb issue in Bosnia, none have been resolved. Everybody believes that the Croats should get their own unit, their own entity, but I believe that the Muslims should get their own unit, their own entity, because the problem is that somebody always wants to lord it over somebody else, and all the three communities should be in an equal position. They used to live together peacefully, but only when there was equality among them. Today, the Croats do not have their own unit, the Muslims do not have their own unit, and they are both against Serbs who do have their own unit. And the hatred was resurrected because those three ethnic communities did not get their opportunity for certain things, that they should have had. I think if certain ambitions that they had had been realised, they would have been able to live in peace. If you had an amount of self-government rather than another nation deciding your fate, I think that would have satisfied each of the three communities. That is my opinion, maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to ask you a question about the 22nd Session and an extract from a speech by Mr. Srdjo Srdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've examined this, and we found two different translations. I know that Mr. Tieger had mentioned to the Chamber that this was a -- this was a session where the Prosecution provided a new translation. Perhaps I could give Mr. Krajisnik the -- this part, the relevant extract.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you could cite the pages, please, in B/C/S and English we could be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In B/C/S it's 02149745, it's page 37. Could that be handed to Mr. Krajisnik, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could that be repeated, please? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the English is concerned, as I say, we have two different translations, one bears a page number 115 at the bottom, the other bears a page number 118 of 123 at the bottom. I don't know whether my learned friend Mr. Tieger can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tieger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 115 in the English is -- appears to be the corresponding text to the B/C/S page cited by my learned friend in what -- in the revised translation, which, simply by its length, I think you can tell is a more helpful translation. So I think that citation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sadly for this particular passage, it is less helpful because it has a number of words as illegible, important words, we say, in the context of this particular speech. I am going to read this, if I may, from the other translation, ask Mr. Krajisnik to follow it closely in the original, and if one of these words is not there or is not clear, perhaps he could say. Mr. Srdic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why don't we have -- assist the translators and interpreters in doing so, which seems to be -- I mean, if there is going to be a question about what's objectively legible and what's not, I mean, they might as well be -- seem to be the most helpful people to follow, and we can try to do the same as well. I certainly share my learned friend's concern that we get all the legible portions translated fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy with that. We've got a number of copies of the original translation. New translation I've just got one that could go on the ELMO. Entirely in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you put it on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The original or the new one, Your Honour? I'd like to read from the original one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it possible to put it in such a way on the ELMO that we have both copies so that we even can compare? I don't know -- of course if the one is at the bottom and the other at the top, then could we try to have them --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Allow me to show the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you indicate to the usher -- if they could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One of these versions I've underlined; the other I have not, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the original which is underlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and if you could move in in such a way that we also see the other one, isn't it? So could you please move it a bit, the text, a bit down, so that we can see -- and perhaps a little bit less enlarged so that we see the other copy as well, Mr. Usher. We now only see one of the copies. The relevant portion of the other one -- yes. If you move on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's both on the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now a little bit further down, please. A little bit more so that we see Mr. Srdic on both. Well, if you read the underlined part -- I take it then, Mr. Josse, you want to -- no. It was fine as it was but let's not -- yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "Prijedor has on average 10 and a half and sometimes even 12.000 soldiers on the front. We will pull them all back from the front lines and we will crush. We did not ask you, nor Mr. Karadzic, nor Krajisnik, what to do in Prijedor. The only green municipality in Bosanska Krajina was Prijedor. If we listened to you, it would still be green. We would still be Krupa, and Prijedor would not be Prijedor. We have dealt with them and packed them with hard stone to where they belong." And then there was applause. Is the word "green", Mr. Krajisnik, clear in your version?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that means Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because apparently it was illegible in some version. Anyway, let's not worry about that. The essence of both translations is exactly the same. What did you take Mr. Srdic to mean in the extract from that speech that received applause?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Srdic was against the deployment of the Canadian Battalion in Banja Luka, and Mr. Koljevic, since he was the contact person for the UNPROFOR, proposed for the Assembly to make a decision favouring a deployment of the Canadian Battalion in Banja Luka. So Mr. Srdic is coming out against this and he says: We didn't ask you, Mr. Koljevic, and we didn't ask Mr. Karadzic or anyone else, about what to do in Prijedor. We did, as we saw fit, because if we had asked you, the municipality would be green to this day. And then he goes on to use some words like "packing them off," and you can interpret them in different ways. But since this is a reference to the departure of a large number of Muslims from Trnopolje, Manjaca, and so on, it could also be interpreted to mean that they had packed their bags and left for the west, but that they in Prijedor had forbidden this Cedo Aleksic from coming back. It's simply a speech in opposition to the deployment of the Canadian Battalion, and he says that they were going to take radical steps. And I thought it was mere words. He was just intent on making his point that he was against the Canadian Battalion; but since his speech was so temperamental and so aggressive, he was applauded by the audience, and we were hard-put to decide how to implement this deal with the UNPROFOR. But one important component of his speech was when he -- is when he says: We didn't ask you what to do, and we will do this and that if you bring those troops. And it's true that, in Prijedor, the police took over, nobody knew when it happened that morning -- I mean, they seized power.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit more detail about these words: "We did not ask you, nor Mr. Karadzic, nor Krajisnik." Was that a comment designed in any way to illustrate the links or lack of links between that municipality and Pale, or did it only relate to the Canadian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a fact, when he says that we had no links with Prijedor. All of that was done by them without consulting anyone. It's a fact, and he states that fact. But all this was in the context of the discussion about the Canadian Battalion, and it's true, this part where he talks about Prijedor, that they liberated it, and that it's no longer a green municipality but a Serb municipality, that they did that all on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to take you, if I may, to P1225, which was a report to the minister of the interior, that you were asked about in the context of the presence of Arkan's men in Pale. And in one part of this report, top of page 3 in the B/C/S, top of page 3 in the English --.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the witness needs it, Your Honour. It's very well it being provided to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Page 3, Mr. Krajisnik. It says, and I'm paraphrasing, that whilst inspecting the Pale public security station, the group of Arkan's men are still present at the Panorama Hotel. Chief Koroman presents that as a solved problem because he's expecting their commander in a couple of days, with whom he would solve it without a problem. Who was Chief Koroman, firstly, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Mr. Malko Koroman. He was chief of police then, and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was he a man you spoke to regularly or at all during the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was quite seldom, but I knew the man, no denying that. I don't even know when I talked to him, but I do not rule out having talked to him. I talked to him but I don't know when. I mean, I had no reason to talk to him often. I talked to him very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did he ever mention to you what is contained within this report, namely that Arkan's men were present at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't, Mr. Josse. I'd like to explain this. The minister was in Pale too, the minister of the MUP, and this Radevic, and the government, all of them, and they were in Panorama together with me. So they all could have seen Arkan's men. There would not have been a debate about refugees at a government meeting, but the question would have been what to do with Arkan's men. I claim that there were no men of Arkan's where I was, maybe there were some refugees. But perhaps this other facility within panorama, Buducnost, where the wounded were, whether they were there, well that's what I don't know. Anyway the minister was there, and Radevic found out only when he went to the police, he heard from Koroman that Arkan's men were there -- although Radevic was in Pale, and the minister and everybody was in Pale. Why would he find out only from him? He could have known, too, that they were in Panorama. I mean, I really don't know about them being there. Nobody ever told me that, and I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the years subsequent to 1992, but prior to your removal from Pale to The Hague, did you ever talk to Mr. Koroman at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I mean -- well, at that time -- I mean later, but never about there problem and he never told me anything about this -- or rather, I never asked him about it. Perhaps he would have said something to me had I asked about it, but I never asked and he never said anything. I mean, I never saw this report either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In tab P1 -- let me start again. In P1224, which is a report also to the minister of the interior and I could show it to you if need be, someone called the chief and commander in SJB Pale is mentioned. Page 3 in the English, top of page 3 in the B/C/S. Who was the chief and commander in the SJB Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Arkan -- oh, my goodness, Mr. Koroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So it's one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. One and the same person. He was chief, and I don't know who the commander was. This report was before the first one -- I mean the one that we discussed earlier on followed after this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The commander and the chief are two different people? The chief was Mr. Koroman; you don't know who the commander was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember who the commander was, but Koroman was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move to tab 268 of the Prosecution presentation. I'm afraid I -- this is the 5th Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BH held on the 10th of June of 1992, and I regret to say I do not have the exhibit number at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's written at the top that it's P64A, tab 730, so that's at least what appears on our --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not on mine, but I'm very grateful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has provided it. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very kind of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, on the last page there is a reference to Dr. Buha. And in the course of your evidence, you were asked about an extract at around that point from these minutes, and you told the Chamber that you wanted to say something to them about Mr. Buha. The learned Judge stopped you, said it wasn't the appropriate time, and it could be dealt with subsequently. I'm now giving you that opportunity to deal with it subsequently, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, I just wanted to indicate something in support of what I said, that these meetings were always attended by more people than actually recorded. See here, it's Mr. Buha. And if you recall, Mr. Djokanovic also testified that he was at that meeting, and he was not recorded as an attendee. That was the point. Now, it looked as if Buha were a member of the Presidency too, or I don't know what, but it just depended on the recording clerk, what he wrote down. That was what I wanted to say with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. One second, please. Yes, I have one question -- it's not at the beginning of the questions by the Bench, but we are just talking about Mr. Koroman. Are you aware of any links between Mr. Koroman and paramilitary units or paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not know, although I saw this evidence here, that those yellow wasps were in Pale once. But at that time, I didn't know about his links to the paramilitary units. That Dzudza came to Pale once. I saw that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first have the break, Mr. Krajisnik, and then questions by the Bench will be put to you. We'll have a break until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Judge Hanoteau will put the first questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, please. I would like to go back to the very beginning of your testimony and I would like you to tell us more about first the environment you were raised in, what kind of family you were raised in, if you don't mind, of course. What your parents were doing, you know, how the family -- the make-up of the family and so on. And you know, whether you were raised in the city or in the country, what school you went to. I'm going all the way, you know, if you let me. And of course what I'm interested in is what you said earlier, you know, you were talking about this plural ethnic society. Were you raised in this pluri-ethnic society? Did your family invite Croats, Muslims? Did you have social relationships? Did you see each other and so on? And then given your age, I'd also like to know when you started to understand that there were tensions between these communities. You talked about this brotherhood that had been maybe covered by a political regime, but was it just a facade, you know, a real brotherhood? How did you experience all this? How did you feel during your childhood, your teenage, until you became an adult, you know, the formative years, if I may say so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in a village. My mother and father had another son, so we were two brothers. And I had several uncles on my father's side and a rather large family. Zabrdje, where I was born, was purely a Serb village, but I went to school to Reljevo village, and that school was one school for the broader area of Rajlovac. It was attended by Serbs, Muslims and Croats. Serbs outnumbered the others but there were others, too. I had friends among them, and I never viewed any schoolmates as anything but friends. I had to walk to school, about four kilometres, and there was another village a bit further up from mine, Smiljevici which was mixed, Serb-Muslim. Our family was a patriarchal one. We believed in God and respected our elders, and we respected the customs of other people, too. When Muslims came to visit - and they don't eat pork - my mother would cook separately for them. She would always say, "This is the table for the Muslims and this is what Croats and Serbs can eat." And we always joked around, saying, "Let's eat the Muslim table first." I frequented Muslim families as well, including the family of a very good friend of mine in Rajlovac who was my schoolmate through primary and secondary school and also the university and later on we worked together. After primary school, I went from Rajlovac to Sarajevo by train, seven or eight kilometres, perhaps. I shuttled every day, and did the same throughout university, and after graduation I found a job with a large company Energoinvest. We were all hard workers in our family. I worked throughout my childhood. I helped around the house and with all the other work, and I was never bothered by it because I believed that one should earn one's living and work for whatever one gets. And our family was rather well off in that area. As for contact with other ethnic communities, my parents brought me up to respect people of other ethnic communities, maybe even more than Serbs, because it is easier to offend people of other communities than your own. Just for example, the attending physician of my wife was a Muslim, whose name I won't mention because I want to keep him from having any unpleasantness in Sarajevo. He called my mother later, asking her to ask me to send some medication for his mother who suffered from asthma. I bought those medicines in Geneva and gave them to the Muslim delegation to take it to him. However, later, when my investigators asked him to make a statement about me, he refused because he said, you know, I don't want to get into trouble. And I was a little disappointed, I must say. Whenever I could help to send a parcel to somebody, to get somebody out of prison, to do whatever, I always did, and I'm not saying this to -- by way of a mitigating factor, because I believe that God sees it all, so I don't need to say that in mitigation. And in answer to your question as to whether I had taken any steps when I heard about crimes, I remembered something yesterday that I want to mention now. A high Muslim representative once told me: Look, there is a brothel somewhere in your area and there is a girl there, a Muslim girl, that I would like you to bring to the airport. I was very surprised. I thought that couldn't be true. I sent somebody over there and indeed they found her. When they -- when they brought her, I asked her whether she had really been in a brothel. She said: Nothing of the kind. I asked whether she had had any problems? She said no. I took a statement from her before sending her on to her father. And anyway, I was happy to have helped because I too have a daughter, and I did the same all my life. You also asked me when, at which moment, I felt intolerance among ethnic communities. I would say that it's not the political parties who caused all the problems when they appeared. It's the moment when all the three ethnic groups felt a kind of freedom; they were free to be Serb, Muslim, or Croat as much as they wished. And at that moment - I have to be honest - at that moment somebody said, "You, gentlemen, Muslims, you can now apply to have your own state." I'm not condemning them, but it's their fault the war started. It was a great temptation for them. All their lives, they were in between two sides; they were a bargaining chip between Serbs and Croats. So they did apply, Bosnia was recognised, and chaos set in. I don't know what I would have done in their shoes, what I would have done if somebody had told me: It takes only one move for you to get a Serbian state. I don't know. But when I became president of the Serb Assembly, I had a lot of ideals about building a society of mutual tolerance and respect and then I saw that everybody was pulling to their own side. I realised there was an invisible hand orchestrating, conducting, all the three sides away from tolerance, away from understanding. Only history will be able to tell. But when we speak about the break-up of Yugoslavia, all our problems from the Ottoman Empire, from long ago history, were resurrected at the moment when a Bosnian state became reality. All the negative things were resurrected, revamped, and conflict ensued. So the answer to your question is: The moment that talks began about an independent Bosnia, the relationships deteriorated a great deal. I was not a member of the League of Communists, but I knew -- I grew up to believe that there are people of other faiths, other ethnic groups, that you have to respect. And when somebody here alleged that I called them Turks during the war, I never wanted to say a bad thing about them, although they were enemies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know what your father was doing. He was a farmer? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father was a farmer and my mother was a housewife. They both had four years of primary school, and the same is true of all my uncles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to come back to what you said on that society that existed before the events that we are dealing with, so before these parties actually were created. Do you think that under the socialist regime, at the time there was repression and it was thanks to repression that these tensions didn't crop up? Was it a police state? Was that what was making this cohesion between -- what looked like cohesion in this society? Was it thanks to the police state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said I was not a member of the League of Communists. I was not a member of the party. But now when everybody is attacking the party, I'm in a position almost to defend it because nobody seems to be -- to have been in favour of the party. Everybody is just attacking it. There was no repression of that kind, Your Honour, but this is what happened. Quite simply, there was no freedom in the true sense of the word. For example, if you'd go to church, if you'd celebrate a holiday, you were branded a black sheep. That didn't go only for the Serbs; it went for all three ethnic communities. Or if you were not a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, you could not get promoted. I was a director though, but I had to work three times as hard in order to prove myself as compared to people who were members of the party. But in principle I did not want to join the party because that would have been an unfair way to get promoted, if I can put it that way. And then if they would find a nationalist, say a Serb, ten days later they would find a Croat, they would find a Muslim, too, so they would say: We are not opposed to anyone in particular, it has to do with all three communities. For example, a man sang a song when his son was born, and then he was sent to prison for 40 days. So that was one of the shortcomings of this socialism. My youth was in the times of socialism, so I cannot say that nice things didn't happen; but quality was not respected in work, only affiliation to this one and only party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I have a second question on what -- on the activities -- your activities after the Dayton agreements. So I would like to know exactly what happened to you right until you were arrested. What happened to you after the Dayton Agreements? What was your employment and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Dayton -- well, first of all I was really bitter in Dayton because Sarajevo was handed over in an unfair way and because I knew that there would be an exodus. When the Main Board of the Serb Democratic Party left -- or rather, the Presidency of the Serb Democratic Party, they were putting forth candidates. Since Karadzic could not be office holder, who would be the Speaker of Parliament? Who would be president of the republic? Who would be president of the party? And who would be a member of the Presidency? Nobody wanted to be a member of the Presidency in Sarajevo at the time. First of all, emotionally, because they thought that after all, Serbs were harmed, Sarajevo was seized from them; and on the other hand they didn't want to quarrel with the Muslim and the Croat representatives and to struggle with them, so to speak. When nobody wanted to take that on, it was very easy for them to reach agreement who would be president of the republic, Speaker of the Assembly. I said: I don't want to be Speaker of the Assembly. I've had enough of that. Quite simply, I want to devote myself to my family and to myself. When no one accepted to be a member of the Presidency, I did. Everybody said: Well, we don't know what it's going to be like for you out there, but I went to Sarajevo and I was there with Mr. Izetbegovic, the late Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Zubak. I spent two years there. I thought that I was supposed to represent Serb interests and I did, to a maximum. But I did not want to harm the other two peoples in any way. They were in coalition, the two of them, and very often they outvoted me. At one moment, Mr. Zubak and I were on one side and Mr. Izetbegovic on the other side. Then we were supposed to take a vote in order to defeat Mr. Izetbegovic, and I said: No, I won't, I will be neutral. I don't want to have any out-voting here. We have to have a joint position, because it's easy to out-vote someone and to create discord. We should make a maximum effort to implement the Dayton Agreement. I did implement a great many things, together with the two of them, that is. After those two years, another person came and then I saw that in fact I had nothing to live on. I had to do something, so since I'm an economist I went into a bit of private business. I started doing something, and then I got this concrete factory and I tried to get a cement factory going, it was very primitive. But I wanted to provide for my family and to make it possible for myself to live on. Throughout the war -- and also, when I was arrested I was in Panorama. I only went to see my parents during the weekend, and they were actually subletting an apartment in a house. Ten days before I was arrested, my relatives who lived upstairs went to their own house that they had built and I was upstairs with my children when I was arrested, so there are many problems left there, credits that have to be repaid, loans -- well, of course my brother and other members of my family are trying to help out. This is a small company, in actual fact, but I think that they are doing their best. My father died; the first Chamber did not allow me to attend the funeral. My mother is old, barely alive. All three of my children finished university in Pale. They got degrees in economics. I couldn't send them away anywhere. I could only afford Pale so they live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, so you decided to leave your political mandate. Did you do that before you started your private business?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were election rules. I was a candidate once again for being a member of the Presidency, but then there were votes within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then there were votes that came in by mail. I won in the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but when the votes from abroad came in, because the Muslims and the Croats and the Serbs had the right to vote -- I'm not trying to say anything, whether this was regular or irregular, but after that -- I don't know how many votes it was that led to the fact that I lost the election and then I went into private business. So I was a candidate for Presidency member for another term, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During those months before your arrest, you knew that there were charges brought against you by the International Criminal Tribunal? You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no indications whatsoever. But I had a degree of psychological pressure there because in front of the building where I worked there was often a SFOR APC, and I wrote a letter to General Adams asking him why this is disturbing me there and if he has anything against me he should tell me. And therefore, people felt uncomfortable to come see me; quite simply, they were afraid. When I was arrested, I couldn't come to. I think that my blood pressure soared to 200 or whatever. I went through all sorts of checks. I mean when you're a candidate you do. It never crossed my mind that I could have been indicted for war crimes here. Actually, in all fairness, if somebody is following you all the time, then you feel sort of uneasy. It's not that you know something, but you simply feel uneasy. However, I simply could not conceive of any such thing that I could have been arrested or charged. Even a high official, I don't want to mention his name, from the international community, with whom I was on good terms, some representatives of Republika Srpska were talking to him once and they said that he had said he is the only one I know was not indicted for war crimes. I wanted him to be a witness for me, but time was brief and therefore we gave up on that because we cooperated on different matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now have a third question for you, Mr. Krajisnik. During the cross-examination of the 29th of May, the Prosecutor stated or quoted something that was said during the 11th Assembly Session and talked about the intervention of Mr. Zekic. Mr. Zekic stated, and I will quote him in English because I found the passage in English. He talks about Muslims. [In English] "With their birth-rate, they will gradually stifle our territories and we will find ourselves in a difficult situation." [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked you a question on that particular sentence, and you answered. Was it a threat for us? No. It was rather our human rights. It was rather the human rights, our human rights, that were threatened. There was enough room for everybody, more than we all needed. And I would like to know if you could kindly elaborate on this. Why was there an eventual threat on your individual rights, whilst if we take into account that everybody was living together, that you were living in a Bosnian Croathood and, as you mentioned, so often that we were used to living together, quote and unquote? So why is there all of a sudden a threat that could threaten people and the rights of those people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just talk about space. Bosnia-Herzegovina is 50.000 square kilometres and the population was 4 million. When I compare this to the Netherlands that has a population of about 17 million and there could have been a population three times bigger, so it wasn't a lack of space that was a problem. The problem was in human rights. In a democracy, if you look at birth-rates and if you are trying to use your numbers in order to out-vote someone and to deny someone else their human rights, that's a problem, when there is more of someone else, when there is not an instrument that could protect a minority. Quite simply, at the beginning of our multi-party activities, if I can put it that way, quite a few people were terrified by that because we couldn't even agree on the oath in the beginning. There was a coalition that was set up straight away, and you feel as if you were a minority. And then when you feel that you're a minority and on the other hand you were a constituent people, then everything that you feel is sacred to you can be taken away from you, symbols, your flag, your alphabet and so on and so forth. I'm saying the birth-rate was not a problem for its own sake. There could have been a population of 15 million. How can somebody blame someone else for not having any more children? Serbs have less children, Muslims have more. But if you abuse that and if you say: I want to have a civil state, and if you know that you want to be 51 per cent, so that you could impose your own authority on others - and on the other hand you have a history, which is the way it is - then you're afraid of that birth-rate. Because due to these numbers, in an irregular way, the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was affected. And also, when they say we cannot live with you Serbs because you're a majority in Yugoslavia and then we say: Well, if you're afraid of us because we are a majority, how are we not going to be afraid of you in Bosnia if you're going to be a majority there? That's the problem of the birth-rate, and it's evident that the Muslims had much bigger families than the Serbs and the Croats did. So if the birth-rate is instrumentalised, not in terms of taking territories, then that turns into a problem. Zekic was a bit more radical but I am saying what turned out to be a problem amongst us when this political life started taking place in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Zekic spoke, well, along the following lines: Before the war, it was a bit local so he was looking at it locally, I think. Srebrenica, such a misfortune now. Through the centuries it went from Serb hands to Muslim hands to Hungarian hands and I don't know, so everybody takes their own point of departure, regardless of whether they are right or not. And he was from Srebrenica and he was a minority there and he was afraid of being a minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow, Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to make a comment. You say, "if the birth-rate was instrumentalised," what do you mean by that exactly? I can't quite follow you. I can't follow your explanation. If you say that the birth-rate is not necessarily instrumentalised, it is what it is and it always is. Birth-rates take place or not. Why do you say that the birth-rate is instrumentalised? Was it instrumentalised? You're talking about Muslims, of course, more than Croats when you say that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croats were in the most difficult position of all, but let me tell you what I was trying to say. The Serbs and the Croats were moving away, moving to Serbia and Croatia. In addition to the low birth-rate, they were leaving, they were going to Serbia and Croatia, whereas the Muslims were moving in and they had a higher birth rate, too. So for the first time when you have a multi-party assembly, and when there are instruments of protecting those who are minority, and then there is someone who goes about this by force -- the Muslims and the Croats had a shared objective and they violated the constitution. So then you wonder: What's going to happen the following day when Bosnia will be a state based on the rule of law and one man, one vote, et cetera? Then what will happen? Bosnia-Herzegovina had all the prerogatives of a state and Yugoslavia too, but we said: All right, if you don't want to be in Yugoslavia, just give us what Bosnia and you had in Yugoslavia. We are going to agree to Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, but let us have some kind of small autonomy where we can exercise our own rights. So we saw in effect what it was like when the majority instrumentalised this, and the majority was due both to the birth-rate and to the fact that Muslims were moving in. If they were 51 per cent - that was our understanding - they would have rejected the Croats; now they needed the Croats because they did not have 51 per cent on their own. We couldn't have done a thing otherwise. We were just seeking instruments of protection. All of that exists nowadays, Your Honour, all of this was introduced after the Dayton Accords. Quite simply, the Croat people have become even smaller than they were before, but there can be no out-voting. You simply have to reach agreement on certain things. You cannot simply impose your own will because there is more of you. That was it. That is what the Serb people were afraid of. Probably the Croat people too, but then I'm speaking about the Serb people because that's what I know about. We couldn't agree on the alphabet, believe me. In the beginning, there was the Serbo-Croat language. All of a sudden it became Croat, Serb, Bosniak and then the letter was -- and then the alphabet, it -- was it Cyrillic? Was it the Roman script? We spent days and days working on unproductive things, if I can put it that way. I would even have to have breaks in the work of the Assembly so that they could go to the mosque to pray. I really made an effort on all scores. I really tried to be helpful to the very end. Unfortunately there had to be a collapse, unfortunately. It's not only the collapse and the war that were a problem, but also the fact that crimes and evil things are remembered for hundreds of years in Bosnia. Today people remember what happened 500 years ago, so the consequences are going to be terrible in the consciousness of the people for years and years on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, a small precision, please. I didn't quite understand an explanation that you just gave us. You said that your first very first project at the onset was to create municipal assemblies, Serbian municipal assemblies. Your goal was not to obtain Serbian territories. Do you recall that sentence? Do you recall uttering that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that we wanted to create assemblies, municipal assemblies, after the statement of Mr. Izetbegovic. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. So I would like to obtain a very clear explanation. I may not have heard it. I may not have understood it. If you take one municipality, for instance, and that municipality is comprised of a main city and many other villages around it, villages or hamlets, within that municipality, therefore, let's imagine that there is a Serbian minority living there. That Serbian minority, I would imagine that before the conflict, which is at the heart of this trial, was -- this Serbian minority was very frequently outvoted in municipal assemblies, in municipal institutions, I suppose. And I believe that that was at the crux of the problem. You wished that that Serbian minority could be protected by institutions that were her -- their own institutions. Did I understand you correctly so far? So if we take this as a hypothetical standpoint, what was happening with the Muslims and the Croats, your Serbian minority is creating institutions in order to be represented, but how the other -- how can the other communities live then? The other communities, are they going to have their own institutions, therefore I'm talking about Croatian institutions and Muslim institutions? And how will these three municipal institutions live together? How will they function? How did you envisage the situation? Could you please clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provided I understood your question, you're talking about Serbs who are a minority in a certain municipality and are being outvoted. We issued clear instructions when the republic Serb Assembly was formed, if I can call it that, then we received initiatives from the municipal level where there was out-voting and coalitions. We instructed them to remain, both officials and deputies, to remain in the Municipal Assembly. And if they form a Serb Assembly, that that Serb Assembly should deliberate only on issues that involve vital Serb interests, like waste depots, like communal things. They should be a council of the people. The Serbs should then say in the common Municipal Assembly: On this issue Serbs do not agree. This is what we think. So it was envisaged that we remain in the Municipal Assembly, but when there is no other recourse, when we disagreed, we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm stopping you here, if you'll allow me. But that was the case already within that municipality, right, the municipality that we are hypothetically talking of? The minority, the Serbian minority, was already represented. So what was a new instrument? What was this new instrument that you were implementing? This is what I would like to understand. The Municipal Assembly was comprised of Muslim, Croat, and Serb representatives. In my -- according to my hypothesis, the Serbs were in the minority and they were able to express themselves within that Municipal Assembly. Let's say that they were out-voted, so I imagine that that could happen, that they could be out-voted, and you wanted to implement something to create an institution, to create an instrument, in order for that not to happen. But what is it that you wanted to create? What is this new instrument that you wanted to create which would allow the Serbs not to be out-voted, so which would prevent the Serbs to be outvoted? I don't understand how you thought this could be done. How did you want to get to this? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the problem, the out-voting; that's a democratic way. The problem was when somebody violated your rights, the rights that you had according to the legislation, to the constitution. In that case the club of Serb deputies would say: "This is the Serb Assembly, and we don't agree with being out-voted against the law." We were out-voted hundreds of times in the Republican Assembly, on a law, on a regulation, on whatever, but when we were outvoted on something that touched on our vital interests, that was the problem. We could not go through with it in the Republic Assembly, but at least our voice could be heard. I'm just explaining what we wanted to do. If somebody rises and says: We want an independent Bosnia. You say: Okay, if it's according to the law, the constitution, but if they want to go against that, then we don't agree. I produced one document here, when Mr. Muhamed Filipovic said in his book: We couldn't do it the legal way, so we went ahead with the referendum. The referendum, however, was not the legal way. The legal way was through the Assembly. The referendum could only show the opinion of the people. So when somebody is violating the rights that you have according to the conventions, the constitution, the law, that was a real problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when this Serb minority is systematically out-voted, and because of this you wished to create an autonomous institution which would represent them entirely; is that correct? You thought that they could create a purely Serb Municipal Assembly which would exist and co-exist with the other Assembly, Municipal Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. So that Club of Deputies would become a Serb Assembly, would discuss a decision on which they had been out-voted, but they still continued to work in the Municipal Assembly. And there is the decision whereby they should continue in their posts because we did not want to overthrow the existing Assembly. But it was our only defence, our last resort, when somebody was violating our rights, it was a way to show that we disagreed, although we couldn't do anything because the Assembly was the only forum that was entitled to make such decisions. However, even that didn't last long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir, and I also have a fifth question for you. I would like you to tell me something about Mr. Davidovic. Mr. Davidovic was a witness, so therefore my question relates to him, and he testified about his presence on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he explained very precisely and very clearly and I will quote him in English. He said: [In English] "Federal secretary to -- Federal SUP secretary told Davidovic that the group of policemen was sent as part of an offer of help from Yugoslav Prime Minister Milan Panic to the leadership of the BS Republic. After the latter had complained that it could not control Serbian paramilitaries in BH, who were killing Muslims and looting." [Interpretation] This quote made by Mr. Davidovic relates to the leadership of the Bosnian Serb Republic; it pertains to that. So what I would like to know from you, Mr. Krajisnik, is if at any point in time you heard, through the people you worked with, that a support was going to be needed from a special federal force to get rid of that problem, the problem of the paramilitaries, was that ever said? Was that ever told -- said directly to you? Did you ever hear about it? Was it ever discussed, either in your presence or outside of your presence? And I'm terribly sorry for making such long sentences or asking such long questions, Mr. Krajisnik. But Mr. Davidovic arrived on the field, he arrived with a mission, he had orders, so how is it -- how can you explain his presence, other than the fact that he was required to come by the authorities of your own republic to put an end to the paramilitaries? And can you therefore say that you were absolutely not aware of the fact that this specialist which would intervene was called? Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Panic only once in the Hyatt Hotel in Belgrade. I saw him only once, although I know him. He was president of Yugoslavia. Never in my life had I seen this Davidovic who testified here, nor did I know that the special units of Serbia or Yugoslavia had been in Republika Srpska. I spoke to some detainees here, and they told me that in Brcko there were some men with red caps. To me, it was all like a tale, like a story. You will have opportunity to hear Mr. Stanisic here. And as for special units of Yugoslavia, if they had been on the territory of Republika Srpska, they had to be invited or brought by somebody. In my immediate circle, Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, I don't think that any of them had asked those special units to come. I never even spoke to that Davidovic. I had seen him maybe in this villa Bosanka in Belgrade. Maybe he was there, but I never had anything to do with him. He said a lot of things that were untrue and that hurt me a lot, about the yellow wasps, about Bijeljina. I don't know whether he was involved in that. He probably was, because there are some documents wherein the municipality of Bijeljina declared him unwelcome. I didn't even know that he was in Pale or in Vrace. I had never heard of that man. I knew other man named Davidovic, but of this one I had never heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one last question pertaining to this, and I will end my questions for today. Today, do you have the feeling that things or events were hidden from you while you were still in power?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm convinced that nothing was kept from me. I'm convinced that I was rather well-informed and that what he's saying is untrue. I may be wrong, but there was no reason for anyone to keep something from somebody else. There was no reason why a minister wouldn't tell me what he was doing. I'm not aware of any reason why somebody would be keeping information from me or other people. There is a record of that government meeting where Mico Stanisic was placed in charge of dealing with things in Bijeljina, and he did indeed go to Bijeljina. Whether he had invited somebody, that he should tell you himself when he comes here. That was not in my province, and I was not even particularly interested in following up on somebody who was going away to do a job. We discussed a lot of things and whatever you might decide to ask me, I will tell you whether somebody had discussed it with me or not. I knew about those yellow wasps in Zvornik, and my information was that it was a special unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska who did that job. I never heard anything about any involvement of any Davidovic. They had intercepted Mr. Ostojic, they mistreated him, together with Mr. Trbojevic, and then he raised it at a government session and they said then that the special unit of the MUP would take care of it. Those two deputies that I'm referring to were intercepted in Zvornik and abused and that's what I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to finish for the day, Mr. Krajisnik. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given or still to be given. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, the 20th of June, Courtroom II, quarter past 2, but I would like to inform the parties that on Thursday, we have a little bit of an irregular schedule. That is we'll start at the normal time but in the morning, then have a bit of a longer break. I think it's from 11, or something like that, to 12.30, and then we'll continue and finish relatively early for the day. It's due to all kind of practical problems we are facing with the scheduling of that day. So this is just to inform you about the irregular times we'll be sitting on Thursday. We will adjourn for the day until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
